interest: This file provides a revealing view into the economic, bureaucratic, and diplomatic complexities of managing occupied Japan's primary export commodity—raw silk—under General Douglas MacArthur's SCAP administration. It documents sharp friction between military headquarters in Tokyo and Washington authorities, vividly illustrated by Representative Daniel J. Flood's defense of silk expert Magagna against what Flood termed obstructionist 'amateur diplomats or amateur economists' on MacArthur's staff. Furthermore, the records demonstrate the intricate mechanics of early postwar multilateral trade, showing how the U.S. Commercial Company tested auction and grading mechanisms, how Commonwealth nations (India, Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom) negotiated raw silk allocations amid acute sterling inconvertibility, and how domestic American textile importers by late 1948 voiced grievances over European purchases subsidized by Marshall Plan dollars.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.6225, filed under the classification for animal husbandry and silk culture in Japan) documents the rehabilitation, pricing, quota allocation, and international marketing of Japanese raw silk during the Allied Occupation between March 1946 and December 1948. Central matters include high-level coordination and inter-agency friction between the State Department, the War Department, and General Douglas MacArthur's SCAP headquarters over the status of civilian silk experts sent to Tokyo; the commercial distribution of Japanese silk stockpiles through the U.S. Commercial Company (USCC) via New York sealed-bid auctions and Japanese grading standards; inter-allied quota negotiations and currency exchange arrangements with Commonwealth nations including India, Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom; and late-1948 protests by American silk importers regarding price increases and large-scale French silk purchases financed indirectly through Marshall Plan funds.

subfiles.about: Representative Daniel J. Flood forwards to Edwin M. Martin a copy of his memorandum to General Hilldring concerning silk expert Magagna's mission to Japan.
subfiles.from: Daniel J. Flood, M.C., U.S. House of Representatives
subfiles.summary: Representative Daniel J. Flood sends a copy of his memorandum addressed to Major General John H. Hilldring to Edwin M. Martin, Chief of the Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs. Flood notes that because General Hilldring is on leave, he has asked Hilldring's secretary at the Pentagon to ensure General Echols attends to it in the War Department. He expresses warm appreciation for the full cooperation received from the State Department and shares the document for Martin's information.
subfiles.title: Letter from Daniel J. Flood to Edwin M. Martin enclosing memorandum to General Hilldring
subfiles.to: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Representative Daniel J. Flood urges General Hilldring to rectify SCAP's misunderstanding regarding silk expert Magagna's War Department affiliation and to end obstructionist interference by SCAP staff in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Daniel J. Flood, M.C., U.S. House of Representatives
subfiles.summary: Representative Daniel J. Flood quotes a radiogram from silk expert Magagna in Tokyo, who complained that SCAP headquarters erroneously claimed he represented the State Department rather than the War Department. Flood clarifies that Magagna was sent as an Army silk expert with State Department concurrence, and he urges Hilldring to instruct SCAP immediately to correct this misperception. Flood sharply criticizes obstructionist 'amateur diplomats or amateur economists' on MacArthur's staff who have prevented Magagna from meeting MacArthur, and he cites Colonel Gross's familiarity with the matter.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Daniel J. Flood to Major General John H. Hilldring regarding Magagna's silk mission to SCAP
subfiles.to: Major General John H. Hilldring, Special Staff, War Department

subfiles.about: The State Department acknowledges receipt of Representative Flood's inquiries concerning investigations into the Japanese silk mission.
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Edwin M. Martin, Chief of the Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, formally responds to Representative Daniel J. Flood's letter of March 29. The surviving text fragment reflects departmental handling and investigations regarding the Japanese raw silk affair. The letter was drafted for Martin's signature by Roswell H. Whitman.
subfiles.title: Letter from Edwin M. Martin to Daniel J. Flood regarding Japanese silk mission inquiries
subfiles.to: Daniel J. Flood, M.C., U.S. House of Representatives

subfiles.about: The Board of Directors of the U.S. Commercial Company discusses whether to market Japanese raw silk through open auctions or sealed bids.
subfiles.from: C. W. Nichols, Division of International Resources, Department of State
subfiles.summary: The USCC Board of Directors met to determine the sales procedure for an upcoming offering of 8,000 bales of Japanese raw silk following an initial sale of 5,350 bales. The Board debated whether to transition immediately to open auctions with upset prices to accommodate the silk trade, or to continue sealed bids because much of the new lot would be sold under Japanese grading rather than United States Testing Company certification. The Board concluded that the sealed-bid method had achieved satisfactory returns and would avoid premature price reductions, voting to maintain sealed bids for the second offering while deferring open auctions for later consideration.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on Sales of Japanese Silk by USCC Board of Directors

subfiles.about: India outlines its two-million-pound raw silk requirement from Japan and agrees to New Zealand's quota if debited against Australia's allocation.
subfiles.from: P. A. Menon, Secretary, India Supply Mission
subfiles.summary: P. A. Menon expresses gratitude for the agreement to increase India's quota of Japanese raw silk to meet its full requirement of two million pounds. He specifies immediate requirements of 700,000 pounds of 20x22 denier and 300,000 pounds of 13x15 denier in grades C through E (or F and G if necessary), while requesting current F.A.S. Japanese port price trends due to falling domestic silk prices in India. Menon also notes India's agreement to a separate 900-bale allocation for New Zealand provided it is deducted from Australia's share.
subfiles.title: Letter from P. A. Menon to Roswell H. Whitman regarding Japanese raw silk allocations for India
subfiles.to: Roswell H. Whitman, Associate Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: The State Department outlines the pricing formula for Japanese raw silk sales to India based on New York USCC auction returns minus shipping and insurance charges.
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Associate Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Roswell H. Whitman explains that Japanese raw silk sold to India should be priced on the basis of average prices realized at recent U.S. Commercial Company auctions in New York, adjusted downward for ocean freight and insurance. He provides specific freight rates from Japan to New York ($8.50 per 100 pounds) and marine and war risk insurance rates (70 cents per $100 of value). He adds that auction price data from September 18 had been furnished to the Agent General for India and SCAP, and notes an impending second auction in New York.
subfiles.title: Letter from Roswell H. Whitman to P. A. Menon regarding Japanese raw silk pricing and freight costs
subfiles.to: P. A. Menon, Secretary, India Supply Mission

subfiles.about: The India Supply Mission confirms its understanding regarding entitlements to purchase Japanese raw silk under announced percentage quotas.
subfiles.from: P. A. Menon, Secretary, India Supply Mission
subfiles.summary: P. A. Menon writes to Roswell H. Whitman concerning the procurement of raw silk from Japan. The letter confirms India's understanding of its entitlement to purchase silk in accordance with previously announced percentage quotas.
subfiles.title: Letter from P. A. Menon to Roswell H. Whitman regarding Japanese raw silk purchase quotas
subfiles.to: Roswell H. Whitman, Associate Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Roswell H. Whitman reports on an inquiry from the New Zealand Legation and submits a draft cable instructing SCAP on payment terms for silk sales to New Zealand.
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Associate Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Roswell H. Whitman reports that Colonel Guy Powles of the New Zealand Legation inquired about the terms and currency for purchasing Japanese silk. Whitman advised him that terms would equal those granted to Australia, with arrangements to be made directly with SCAP in Tokyo. The memorandum includes a draft telegram instructing SCAP to offer New Zealand the Australian payment arrangement pending an agreement on sterling convertibility, citing the Bank of New Zealand dollar selling rate of $3.22 per New Zealand pound.
subfiles.title: Office Memorandum from Roswell H. Whitman proposing telegram to SCAP on silk sales to New Zealand
subfiles.to: A-H - JK Secretariat, Department of State

subfiles.about: R. O. Easton reports that War Department clearance has been obtained for the proposed terms of Japanese silk sales to New Zealand.
subfiles.from: R. O. Easton, Department of State
subfiles.summary: R. O. Easton informs Ernest A. Gross that the New Zealand Legation requested terms and conditions for purchasing Japanese raw silk and was advised that terms would match Australia's through direct arrangements with SCAP. Easton confirms that War Department clearance was secured through Lieutenant Colonel Nagle and recommends Gross's approval of the proposed telegram.
subfiles.title: Office Memorandum from R. O. Easton to Ernest A. Gross regarding silk sales to New Zealand
subfiles.to: Ernest A. Gross, Department of State

subfiles.about: The State Department instructs SCAP Tokyo to offer New Zealand the same silk sales and payment terms provided to Australia pending sterling convertibility agreements.
subfiles.summary: The State Department cables SCAP in Tokyo regarding the New Zealand Legation's inquiry on currency terms for purchasing Japanese raw silk. The telegram advises SCAP to offer New Zealand the payment plan given to Australia pending an acceptable agreement with the British on convertibility of sterling into dollars after six months. It notes that the New Zealand Legation is instructing Wellington to communicate directly with SCAP, and cites the Bank of New Zealand exchange rate for dollars.
subfiles.title: Telegram from State Department to SCAP Tokyo on terms of silk sales to New Zealand
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP, Tokyo)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording British Embassy correspondence on pricing and charges for raw silk shipments from Japan to the United Kingdom.
subfiles.from: J. A. E. Smart, British Embassy, Washington
subfiles.summary: A Department of State cross-reference sheet records incoming correspondence dated December 13, 1946, from J. A. E. Smart of the British Embassy to Roswell H. Whitman. The inquiry, submitted on behalf of the British Board of Trade, addressed deductions from U.S. auction prices to determine f.o.b. Japan prices for raw silk shipments. The document indicates distribution to USCC official Joyce and departmental officers.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for letter from J. A. E. Smart regarding British raw silk purchases from Japan
subfiles.to: Roswell H. Whitman, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Attorney William S. Culbertson conveys client concerns regarding an impending Japanese silk price hike and large-scale French purchases funded under the Marshall Plan.
subfiles.from: William S. Culbertson, Culbertson, Aitchison & Briggs
subfiles.summary: Attorney William S. Culbertson quotes a letter from his client, silk importer Siber Hegner & Co., reporting information gathered in Tokyo by Wolfgang E. Siber/Wagner. The client reported that SCAP planned a 10 percent price increase on Japanese raw silk effective January 1, 1949, and had suspended other sales pending a large, discounted purchase by the French Government funded by Marshall Plan dollars. Culbertson conveys the grievance of American silk manufacturers that French purchases subsidized by U.S. funds were monopolizing available grades and handicapping American consumers.
subfiles.title: Letter from William S. Culbertson to William J. McCornick regarding Japanese silk prices and French purchases
subfiles.to: William J. McCornick, Division of Commercial Policy, Department of State

subfiles.about: The State Department clarifies that it has no report of an impending Japanese silk price rise and is investigating reports of market preemption by French purchases.
subfiles.from: Merrill C. Gay, Assistant Chief, Division of Commercial Policy, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Merrill C. Gay replies to William S. Culbertson's letter concerning a rumored 10 percent increase in Japanese raw silk prices and alleged French monopolization of supplies. Gay explains that the State Department has received no notice of an impending price rise, although SCAP is expected to make an announcement upon the expiration of the guaranteed price period on January 1, 1949. He expresses skepticism regarding reports that French purchases were foreclosing the market to other buyers and confirms that the Department has requested clarification from SCAP in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Letter from Merrill C. Gay to William S. Culbertson regarding Japanese silk prices and French purchases
subfiles.to: William S. Culbertson, Culbertson, Aitchison & Briggs

subfiles.about: The State Department advises the British Embassy that f.o.b. Japan silk prices should be negotiated directly with SCAP in Tokyo and agrees to supply U.S. auction price lists.
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Associate Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Roswell H. Whitman replies to J. A. E. Smart's letter of December 13 regarding deductions from U.S. auction prices to determine f.o.b. Japan prices for raw silk purchased by the British Board of Trade. Whitman advises that pricing formulas and agreements are properly negotiated in Tokyo, where SCAP has authority to conclude contracts with foreign trade missions, and promises to query SCAP about understandings reached on initial UK shipments. He also confirms that Mr. Joyce of the U.S. Commercial Company will regularly provide the British Embassy with price lists from U.S. auctions.
subfiles.title: Letter from Roswell H. Whitman to J. A. E. Smart regarding Japanese raw silk pricing for the United Kingdom
subfiles.to: J. A. E. Smart, British Embassy, Washington
